I'm mainly talking about massively multiplayer online games. It seems like everyone demands they all have official forums, and in the past when I've worked on projects and suggested they weren't necessarily the most critical use of development resources, the reaction has been pretty strong.

I don't understand this. As I recall, the big three MMORPGs of the 90s (Ultima Online, Everquest, Asheron's Call) did not have official forums. Instead, fansites quickly arose to fill the void. It benefits the people who run the fansites because they get more traffic. It benefits the developers because they don't have to spend resources setting up and running the site. It benefits users because if they don't like how one site is run, they can find or make another.

There are businesses like reddit and voat that are completely specialized in running forums and social networks. Why can't game devs focus on making games instead of running forums? Yes, the authentication systems would not be shared between the game and forums, but I don't see how that's such a big deal.
CMV:The expectation that every website with a community should provide its own communication channels is unreasonable.

Official forums don't just provide a venue for players to talk to other players, they also provide a venue for communication between developers and players. Not only does it make it easier for developers to engage with players with regards to meta-portions of their service, they're the only practical way for players to make themselves heard. Moreover, they're practically a necessity in the era of the modern large-scale beta, because while tickets etc. can go a long way they don't afford the kind of discussion that a message board does.

Perhaps new MMOs should consider outsourcing the process somewhat, but there are very good reasons they should still be an official part of it.
No reason why the devs can't participate in fan-run forums.

A dozen or more of them with different rules, processes and management? Not likely. Moreover, that kind of thing often creates nightmares on the business side of things, especially compared to having a single "official" line supplemented by fan-run sites (which is what happens now, for the most part).

I guess you have a point that it can be advantageous to have a place to discuss customer service issues in that way. If this was reddit I'd give you a delta for that.

But as far as general game feedback? Could do an occasional iama to find out what's on players minds. Could have the players elect some delegates to represent them (Star Wars Galaxies did that for awhile.) Announcements from the devs to players could be done through the site or through the game itself. Heck, the devs could make occasional appearances in game.

Sure - that's what I meant by outsourcing: partner with a social media concern to handle such things. That said, I do think that the BBS format is close to ideal for such things, making Reddit etc. relatively poor choices (and, since those are comparatively simple to implement/manage, we tend to see them done in-house). The key point is that there has to be a specific official channel for discourse between the community and developers/company, ideally one which permits community discourse as well (since that tends to dramatically increase participation and leads to some level of self-management).

The actions of the officers fall into a grey area for me; legal, but not arguably unnecessary. I don't think anyone should have gone to jail or lost their job over this one (especially since it's very probably going to have some financial consequences for them), but I think scenarios like these shed light on a shortcoming in how our police forces assess and manage less-lethal threats to themselves and others.

At the end of the day, this man had two good-sized rocks. Not a gun, not a knife, but two rocks. While these were very capable of causing injury, the likelihood of death resulting from these was incredibly low. The probability of a deadly result diminished even further at the time he was fatally shot, as he only had one rock at that time. I think the relative ease of apprehending him alive coupled with the relatively (almost negligible) low lethal threat he posed to the officers and bystanders with said rock justified the risk of injury over the use of lethal force.

But as the saying goes, "I suppose it is tempting, if the only tool you have is a hammer, to treat everything as if it were a nail."

In my eyes, this man would still be alive if the scene had been properly controlled, surrounded instead of having a path of escape. One or all of the officers would have had a shield and/or a helmet to even further diminish the threat posed by the rock, one or more officers would have been armed with less-lethal rubber bullets or bean-bags (though with him being high on meth, it's hard to say if these would have proven effective), and he would have been apprehended with rapid dominance and taken into custody.
